analysis.one_liner: Makes polluters pay federal cleanup costs for a wider range of contaminants under Superfund.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Schatz with one cosponsor, was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Superfund law makes companies pay to clean up releases of 'hazardous substances.' Courts have read that list narrowly, so when companies release other pollutants or contaminants, taxpayers often cover the response costs instead. This bill would make the responsible companies liable for those federal cleanup costs whenever the government actually mounts a response, though it would not allow claims for damage to natural resources from those substances. It never moved beyond a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities near contaminated sites and taxpayers generally, because companies responsible for a release — including releases of pollutants and contaminants outside the current hazardous-substance list — would bear the government's cleanup costs instead of the public. It also helps people whose water or land is contaminated by substances not currently covered, since a federal response would trigger polluter liability.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near contaminated sites

how_it_helps.text: Amends CERCLA so that liability for response costs attaches not only to 'hazardous substances' but also to 'pollutants or contaminants' whenever the President takes a response measure under the Act's response authority with respect to those substances [S2] [S3].

This closes a gap left by court rulings that read CERCLA's coverage narrowly, shifting the cost of responding to a broader set of contaminant releases from federal and state taxpayers to the parties responsible for the release [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies responsible for releasing pollutants or contaminants that trigger a federal response — chemical manufacturers, industrial waste generators, refiners, and other polluters — would pay response costs they currently avoid.

drawbacks.text: The bill expressly exempts liable parties from damages for injury to, destruction of, or loss of natural resources from releases of these pollutants or contaminants, so it creates new cleanup-cost liability while leaving public resources unprotected against damage claims for the same releases [S2] [S3].

Liability attaches only when the President takes a response measure under the Act, so releases the government does not respond to would generate no new liability, limiting how far the expansion reaches [S2] [S3].

Broadened retroactive-style liability raises costs for firms handling waste legally under past practices, a standard industry objection to Superfund expansions; opponents argue this raises prices and deters remediation of marginal sites.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core effect — making the party responsible for a contaminant release pay the government's cleanup bill instead of taxpayers — is a straightforward polluter-pays fix with real benefit to the public and no direct cost to ordinary people. But it is a half-measure: it carves out natural-resource damage claims entirely for these substances and keys liability to a federal response decision, so the strongest critique is not that it goes too far but that it does not go far enough.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which took no action on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the bill on January 16, 2014, joined by Sen. John Rockefeller, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day [S1] [S3] [S5].
The action history shows no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind after the referral through the end of the 113th Congress [S5].
The bill's sole cosponsor was a Democrat, and no companion action is recorded in the House [S4] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that release pollutants or contaminants outside the Superfund's hazardous-substance list, and their insurers, are better off because the liability expansion died in committee; taxpayers remain the default payer when the government responds to those releases.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Industrial polluters who avoid cleanup liability

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.role: U.S. Senator from Hawaii; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend CERCLA liability to pollutants and contaminants and referred it to committee.

for.name: Sen. John Rockefeller
for.role: U.S. Senator from West Virginia; cosponsor

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 16, 2014 and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both supporters were Democrats (the sponsor and one cosponsor), and the bill drew no Republican cosponsors; the committee controlled by the Senate majority did not act on it.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers and industrial waste generators
industries.note: If it had passed, these companies would owe federal response costs for releases of pollutants and contaminants that trigger government action, costs now borne by taxpayers. The industry's savings come directly at the public's expense, though the bill's natural-resource-damage carve-out would have spared them a separate category of liability.
Broader liability means more government-funded responses and more polluter-financed cleanup work, expanding demand for remediation services. Their gain tracks public benefit from cleaner sites.
